description: A tall perennial herb 2-4 m with long lanceolate leaves on leafy reed-like shoots rising from a thick rhizome. Flowers are borne on trailing panicles near the ground and develop into green, three-chambered capsules with small, aromatic, dark seeds.
cultural_significance: Called the 'Queen of Spices', cardamom flavours sweets, tea, rice and festive dishes in India, and is offered in some ceremonies. Ela is part of the classical aromatic group Trijataka and Chaturjata.
habitat: Shady, humid evergreen forests of the Western Ghats between 600 and 1500 m, with rich, moist, humus-rich soil.

uses.title: Digestion, nausea and vomiting
uses.detail: Ela is described as Deepana and is used to prevent nausea and heaviness; often added to rich foods and tea.

uses.title: Cough, throat and respiratory complaints
uses.detail: Seeds with honey or in decoctions are traditional for cough and breathlessness; described as Kapha-Vata hara.

uses.title: Mouth freshening
uses.detail: Seeds are chewed after meals for fragrance and to ease the heaviness of food (Mukhashodhana).

uses.title: Urinary comfort
uses.detail: Classical texts list Ela under Mutrala and use it in painful or scanty urination (Mutrakrichchhra).

uses.title: Aroma and antioxidant studies
uses.detail: Laboratory studies of cardamom essential oil and extracts show antioxidant and digestive effects; human evidence is limited.

preparations.name: Ela churna (seed powder)
preparations.method: Remove the husk and grind the seeds.
preparations.note: Used in Eladi churna and numerous formulations.

preparations.name: Cardamom tea
preparations.method: Crush a pod and steep it in hot water or tea.

preparations.name: Elaadi vati
preparations.method: Classical lozenge with cardamom and other herbs.
preparations.note: Traditionally for cough, throat irritation and nausea.

preparations.name: Ela kwatha
preparations.method: Boil crushed pods in water and strain.
preparations.note: Traditionally used in digestive and urinary complaints.

precautions: Food amounts are safe for most people; medicinal quantities may worsen gallstone colic as cardamom can stimulate bile flow. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy. May rarely cause allergic dermatitis. Use caution with blood thinners in high amounts.

cultivation.climate: Humid tropical hills; 10-35 C with 1500-4000 mm rain
cultivation.soil: Rich, moist, humus-rich forest loam, pH 5-6.5
cultivation.propagation: Seeds or suckers; plant in monsoon
cultivation.harvest: Hand-pick ripe green capsules at intervals and dry them

conservation_status: Not threatened; widely cultivated. Wild populations are in the Western Ghats.
fun_fact: Cardamom is the world's third most expensive spice after saffron and vanilla because the capsules are picked by hand.

regions.name: Malabar Coast
regions.note: Kerala's Idukki hills grow most Indian cardamom
